firstDiff: Students' influence may also differ across the decisions within an inquiry. In a Grade 7 Science and Technology project, students chose to investigate Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women and Girls and developed a public Red Dress exhibition. Their sense of ownership coexisted with accounts of peers overlooking some ideas during collaboration (Jao et al., 2026). In another Grade 7 classroom, concerns about how a community survey might affect respondents became part of the criteria students and adults used to judge a responsible investigation (Krishnamoorthy et al., 2026). Choosing an inquiry topic offers one form of influence. As the work develops, the authority to determine what counts as a responsible investigation may be negotiated again. The two cases bring those later decisions into view, including whether students' concerns can change the criteria guiding the work.

-

Authority is also shaped by what the classroom recognizes as legitimate knowledge and action. Productive disciplinary engagement connects student authority with responsibility to peers and access to resources for investigating a problem (Engle & Conant, 2002). Rightful presence brings a further concern into view, asking how historically unequal relations shape whose ways of knowing are recognized and whose challenges to classroom norms can have consequences (Calabrese Barton & Tan, 2020). The authority exercised through disciplinary standards can be less visible than the choices students make among activities. Participation also depends on whether students can question the criteria by which their explanations are judged.

-

Collaborative professional learning can develop teachers' attention to students' epistemic practices (Shim & Thompson, 2022) and create opportunities to design instructional materials together (Jao & McDougall, 2015). The focus of that work also shapes what becomes available for reconsideration. In rehearsals of mathematical defining, prospective teachers and teacher educators concentrated on pedagogical issues, with few opportunities to discuss students' reasoning about definitions (Kobiela et al., 2023). This emphasis shows how opportunities to examine students' disciplinary thinking can remain limited even in activities designed to support teachers' learning.

Authority is also shaped by what the classroom recognizes as legitimate knowledge and action. Productive disciplinary engagement connects student authority with responsibility to peers and access to resources for investigating a problem (Engle & Conant, 2002). In a sixth-grade geometry classroom, students' concepts developed alongside their participation in proposing and revising mathematical definitions, with the teacher supporting their growing agency in this disciplinary work (Kobiela & Lehrer, 2015). Rightful presence brings a further concern into view, asking how historically unequal relations shape whose ways of knowing are recognized and whose challenges to classroom norms can have consequences (Calabrese Barton & Tan, 2020). The authority exercised through disciplinary standards can be less visible than the choices students make among activities. Participation also depends on whether students can question the criteria by which their explanations are judged.

+

Teachers' interpretations may themselves become objects of inquiry when colleagues work together. In a four-year professional learning community, high school science teachers developed their attention to students' epistemic practices and evidence-based explanations (Shim & Thompson, 2022). A Grade 9 Applied Mathematics initiative offers a different view of collaboration, with teachers reporting learning from the joint development of classroom materials (Jao & McDougall, 2015). The focus of collaboration shapes what becomes available for reconsideration, from the design of instructional materials to the interpretation of students' explanations. The connection to classroom authority lies in how those judgments influence the work students can pursue.

An unexpected student question can bring disciplinary evaluation and classroom authority into the same interaction. The teacher considers the scientific explanation involved while deciding how the lesson might proceed. The grounds offered for that decision, and students' opportunities to respond, shape whether the question becomes part of the class's inquiry.
